content: The integration of clinical, laboratory, pharmacy, and other healthcare data into a unified system is essential for effective patient monitoring and care. This system relies on person-based records that are linked to death registry data, enabling comprehensive tracking and follow-up of individuals through the use of unique identifiers. The implementation of unique identifiers for person-centered monitoring of HIV services follows an incremental pathway. While the order of implementation steps may vary, certain foundational elements must be established before further improvements can be made. The starting point and priorities for implementation depend on findings from a situational analysis, as well as the feasibility and practicality of the proposed changes. In Thailand and the Western Cape Province of South Africa, advanced use of unique identifiers has been achieved for person-centered care. In Thailand, all citizens are assigned a 13-digit personal identification number (PID) at birth, which is managed by the Ministry of the Interior. This PID is used to link data on HIV treatment and care, which is stored in a centralized, web-based Disease Management Information System (DMIS) under the National AIDS Programme. In the Western Cape Province, the unique identifier system builds on existing electronic identification and information systems. A provincial unique patient identifier is electronically linked to hospital information systems, primary healthcare facilities, and supporting systems such as laboratories, pharmacies, and radiology. The long-term goal is to create a longitudinal, citizen-centered health record that integrates electronic prescribing, test result viewing, appointment scheduling, and health analytics. This system begins with paper records at the facility level, which are entered into an electronic register at the district level and aggregated into a centralized database at the provincial level. The data is used for individual and program management, including tracking loss to follow-up, viral load monitoring, and de-duplication of health records. The development of unique identifier systems involves several stages. Initially, names in paper records are replaced with anonymous codes linked to unique identifiers. The advanced stage expands the system to capture and store all information related to an individual’s interactions across various health services and facilities, including HIV testing, laboratory results, and pharmacy records. Interoperability is a critical component of health information systems, enabling different systems to communicate, exchange data, and use the shared information effectively. Achieving interoperability requires adherence to data exchange standards, open-source solutions, and robust IT infrastructure. Countries must define and enforce national standards for interoperability to address challenges such as fragmented data systems and limited communication between different sources of health data. Privacy, confidentiality, and security are fundamental to the success of health information systems. Unique identifiers enhance anonymity and reduce risks associated with name-based records. Differentiated access and security protocols should be implemented to protect sensitive information, such as names and contact details. The transition from paper-based to electronic systems is a crucial step in managing the complexity of individual care and program management. This transition involves uploading information labeled with unique identifiers or directly entering data into electronic systems. The advanced stage includes fully online systems that can be used across facilities and in community care settings. Sustainability of program improvements requires robust planning and investment in policies, maintenance, hardware, software, human resources, and analytical capacity. To maximize the benefits of unique identifiers, systems must include features such as alphanumeric identifier schemes, secure databases, encryption mechanisms, and administrative infrastructure. These systems must also address issues of confidentiality and security, particularly as the scale-up of health services leads to the collection of increasing amounts of personal health information. Finally, effective national health information systems should support data sharing across clinics, hospitals, laboratories, and pharmacies, regardless of the application or vendor.
